text:
acme-ops: Hey, heads up — since we scaled our private pool yesterday users intermittently see TLS handshake failures and 502s when hitting our Redwood private endpoint. Streaming sessions drop mid-response. Started ~02:30 UTC after an autoscale event.

support-bot: Incident created: #INC-34105. Assigning to oncall. Please attach tcpdump, curl output, and VPC flow logs.

anya: sorry you're hitting this — can you paste a short repro (curl) and any tcpdump showing the handshake / reset? Also which AZ and subnet?

acme-ops: repro: `curl -v --http2 https://private-infer.acme.internal/v1/stream --header "Authorization: Bearer <redacted>"`
curl output:
```
* Connected to private-infer.acme.internal (10.10.4.12) port 443 (#0)
* TLS handshake: TLSv1.3, alert 80
* SSL connect error: SSL: error:14094410:SSL routines:ssl3_read_bytes:tlsv1 alert unknown ca
* Closing connection 0
```
we also see intermittent `read: Connection reset by peer` during streaming frames. Happening from clients in multiple AZs (a & c).

mike.network: thanks. Can you share a 30s tcpdump on the host (client side) showing the full 3-way + TLS? Also paste a snippet of the subnet's NACL and SG. My first guess: asymmetric NAT or ephemeral source port rotation across multiple NATs causing server responses to land on a different 5-tuple. If NACLs are stateless and missing matching ephemeral rules, return packets get dropped.

acme-ops: tcpdump (trimmed):
```
10:02:13.123456 IP 10.20.3.45.52344 > 10.10.4.12.443: Flags [S], seq 12345, win 64240
10:02:13.123459 IP 10.10.4.12.443 > 10.20.3.45.52344: Flags [S.], seq 54321, ack 12346
10:02:13.123789 IP 10.20.3.45.52344 > 10.10.4.12.443: Flags [.], ack 54322
10:02:14.223000 IP 10.10.4.12.443 > 10.20.3.46.33211: Flags [S.], seq 9001, ack 4000
10:02:14.223010 IP 10.20.3.46.33211 > 10.10.4.12.443: Flags [.], ack 9002
10:02:20.500000 IP 10.10.4.12.443 > 10.20.3.45.52344: Flags [R], seq 6000, win 0
```
note the server sends a RST to 10.20.3.45.52344 after earlier traffic, but we also see similar flows to .46 with different source port mapping.

sam: that pattern (responses to different client ports / different client IPs) + RSTs strongly suggests SNAT rotation across multiple NAT gateways or ephemeral port reuse with conntrack misses. Do you use per-subnet NAT gateway with EIP failover?

acme-ops: yes we have one NAT per AZ. After autoscale some flows show the NAT EIP changed between initial SYN and later frames (we saw it in VPC flow logs).

mike.network: right — if the server expects packets to return to NAT1 (src EIP A, port X) but later sees a packet referencing EIP B/port Y due to hairpinning or asymmetric path, conntrack/5-tuple mismatch can result in RST or handshake failures. On top of that, if your NACL denies inbound ephemeral ports (high-range), the server->client packets may be dropped. Remember: NACLs are stateless so you must allow both directions for the ephemeral range.

jordan: can you paste your NACL rules? Especially entries for port 1024-65535 or custom ephemeral range.

acme-ops: NACL for private-subnet-1:
```
Rule 100 ALLOW TCP 443 443 10.0.0.0/8
Rule 110 ALLOW TCP 1024 1024 0.0.0.0/0
Rule 120 DENY ALL    -   -    0.0.0.0/0
```
we realised rule 110 only allowed a single port 1024 not the full ephemeral range. Whoops.

anya: that explains it — if outbound traffic is using ephemeral ports above 1024 (e.g., 32k+), replies will be dropped by the NACL because no corresponding inbound rule exists. Two corrective paths:
- Short term: expand NACL to allow TCP 32768-65535 both inbound and outbound for the client subnets.
- Mid term: adopt a single managed NAT per private endpoint (or NAT with sticky EIPs) so source port/EIP rotation is minimized, and add correct ephemeral range in NACLs.

mike.network: also check your SGs — security groups are stateful, so you only need outbound allow on 443 and the return is allowed. But if you have a host OS firewall (iptables) dropping packets based on conntrack timeouts, that can amplify the issue.

acme-ops: SG snippet: `sg-private: outbound 0.0.0.0/0 tcp 443, inbound 10.0.0.0/8 tcp 443`
host iptables: `DROP all -- anywhere anywhere state INVALID` — no obvious filtering.

sam: recommended immediate steps we rolled out for other customers:
1) update NACL inbound & outbound to allow TCP 32768-61000 (or 32768-65535) for your source CIDR.
2) ensure NAT gateway per AZ has stable EIP allocation (avoid changing EIPs during scale) or use centralized NAT with high port capacity.
3) enable VPC flow logs + capture for a minute to verify symmetric 5-tuple for the failing flows.
4) if TLS alert mentions CA/ALPN, capture full TLS ClientHello for inspection (we saw earlier `tlsv1 alert unknown ca` in one trace — may be a separate client trust issue).

acme-ops: applied NACL change to allow 32768-65535 inbound/outbound. We also pinned NAT EIPs for the AZ. Re-testing now.

(5 min pass)

acme-ops: update — after NACL + NAT pin fix, streaming sessions stable for 30m, no TLS handshake alerts. Looks resolved. Thanks all :raised_hands:

anya: great. We'll close the incident after another hour of monitoring. We'll also add a doc snippet explaining "NACLs + ephemeral ports + NAT rotation" to the Private deployment checklist.

support-bot: Incident #INC-34105 marked: monitoring. Tags: network,nacl,ephemeral-ports,nat
